questions.q: How do single-line (--) and block (/* */) comments behave across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL?
options: Identically — this is one of the rare areas with zero divergence across all four dialects
T-SQL uses // instead of --
Oracle requires a different character for single-line comments
MySQL doesn't support block comments at all
questions.explain: Comment syntax (-- and /* */) is identical across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.

questions.q: Is a semicolon strictly required to terminate most single statements in T-SQL?
options: Historically no, though it's increasingly recommended, and some newer syntax like CTEs actually requires it
T-SQL doesn't support semicolons at all
Only INSERT statements require a semicolon in T-SQL
Yes, it has always been strictly mandatory for every statement
questions.explain: T-SQL has historically allowed omitting the semicolon for most statements, but it's increasingly recommended, and required before a CTE's WITH keyword.

options: A batch separator understood only by SQL Server client tools like SSMS and sqlcmd — not part of the SQL language itself
An Oracle-specific command for committing transactions
A standard SQL keyword supported by all major database platforms
A synonym for COMMIT in T-SQL
questions.explain: GO is purely a tooling convention recognized by SSMS and sqlcmd to split a script into batches; the SQL Server engine itself doesn't understand it as SQL syntax.

questions.q: What happens if you paste a script containing GO into Oracle's SQL*Plus or PostgreSQL's psql?
options: It works identically to SQL Server, since GO is a universal SQL standard
It automatically converts GO into a semicolon
It silently does nothing and continues
A syntax error, because GO is not recognized SQL syntax or a command those tools understand
questions.explain: GO is specific to SSMS/sqlcmd. Neither Oracle's SQL*Plus nor PostgreSQL's psql recognizes it, so it produces a syntax error.

questions.q: Do Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL effectively require a semicolon to terminate statements?
options: Yes, especially once a script or context has more than one statement
Only Oracle requires it; MySQL and PostgreSQL never do
No, none of them ever require a semicolon
Only MySQL requires it; Oracle and PostgreSQL never do
questions.explain: Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all effectively require the semicolon to separate statements, particularly in multi-statement scripts.
